12635-the-philippine-islands-1493-1803-v:
Volume four of The Philippine Islands, 1493-1898, edited by Blair and Robertson, covers 1576 to 1582 in travels, tales, histories and Catholic mission records. Contents include expeditions to Borneo, Jolo and Mindanao, and letters of Francisco de Sande from Manila in 1578 and 1579. Appointments in Manila cathedral by Felipe II in 1580, and a letter from Gonçillo Ronquillo de Peñalosa in 1581, follow.

An ordinance restricting departure from the islands follows, with other papers on politics, trade and church life. The series puts old books and manuscripts into English, showing the islands from first European contact toward the nineteenth century. This volume offers primary sources for early Spanish Philippines, in English, with scholarly care.
12734-the-young-engineers-in-colorado-or:
H. Irving Hancock's Young Engineers in Colorado, or At Railroad Building in Earnest, follows Gridley boys turned cub engineers at a railroad camp. Chapters run from the cub engineers reaching camp and Bad Pete becoming worse through a day of real work. Trying out the Gridley boys, Tom minding artillery, a bite from the bush and what a squaw knew follow.

Gene Black the trouble-maker, doctored field notes, and a chief tottering from command follow. A cub becoming acting chief, plots opening with a bang, a camp shut off from the world and a trap at the finish close the book. Hancock writes brisk boys' adventure, mixing engineering work with villainy. The book is a lively tale of railroads, loyalty and grit.
13120-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume six of The Philippine Islands, 1493 to 1898, covers the years 1583 to 1588, edited and annotated by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson. The series draws on early navigators, island descriptions, and Catholic mission records to show political, economic, and religious life. An introduction by Edward Gaylord Bourne frames the volume.

Chapters treat Manila's spiritual affairs, city matters, trade, forts, soldiers, and expeditions. One passage describes an attack in open ground, where arquebusiers and pikemen advance while townsfolk cry to arms and are disbelieved. Another sets terms for a commander to draw troops, money, and ships from India. The volume is a scholarly source book, not a narrative history.
13255-the-philippine-islands-1493-1803-v:
Volume one of The Philippine Islands, 1493 to 1898, covers 1493 to 1529, edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, with an introduction by Edward Gaylord Bourne. It opens with a general preface, Bourne's history, and documents on the line of demarcation, including papal bulls of 1493 such as Inter Caetera. The series draws on early navigators and mission records.

Papal letters promise success to a saintly undertaking for the happiness of Christendom, and order that notarized copies carry the same weight in court as originals. Later terms bar Portugal from building in Spanish seas, and set penalties from the day subjects are notified. The volume is a documentary foundation for Philippine history, dense with law, faith, and empire.
13280-the-philippine-islands-1493-1803-v:
Volume two of The Philippine Islands, 1493 to 1803, covers 1521 to 1569, edited by Blair and Robertson with notes by Bourne. Contents include the Loaisa expedition of 1525 to 1526, Saavedra's voyage of 1527 to 1528, and Villalobos's expedition of 1541 to 1548, each from contemporary documents. The volume tracks Spain's slow approach to the islands.

One passage tells of a ship-boy killed asleep in a palm grove while water butts were filled, and of four natives seized, three hanged where he died. Another urges priests and laborers for the Lord's vineyard, claiming conversions would come easily, since islanders lack temples and rites. The volume is a raw documentary record, with violence and mission zeal side by side.
13616-the-philippine-islands-1493-1803-v:
Volume three of the fifty-five volume Philippine Islands series, edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, covers the years 1569 to 1576 through documents of the time. Letters to King Felipe II from Cebu, reports on Luzon, and accounts of early Spanish settlement give the story in the words of those who lived it.

Readers meet the first governors, clashes with Portuguese fleets off the islands, and descriptions of peoples, gold mines, and customs, including notes on Muslim settlers called Moros. The editors add introductions and notes to place each paper. As a source collection it is prized by historians of the Philippines, since it prints the raw record of conquest and mission work rather than a later retelling.
13701-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Blair and Robertson's series on the Philippines continues here with documents from 1588 to 1591. Volume seven prints reports, letters, and mission records from the early Spanish colony. Governors describe Manila, trade with Chinese merchants, and trouble with local rulers. Missionaries report on baptisms, schools, and disputes with civil officers.

Notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne place each document in its setting. Readers see a colony short of men and money, yet eager to tax and convert. Chinese residents, called Sangleys, appear as traders, craftsmen, and converts. The volume gives raw evidence for historians of empire, trade, and religion. It rewards readers who prefer sources to summaries.
13742-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited this vast series on the Philippines under Spanish rule. Volume eight covers the years 1591 to 1593 and prints documents from that early period. The sources include reports by governors, bishops, and missionaries, plus records of trade and town life. Edward Gaylord Bourne added historical notes to set each document in context.

Readers meet debates over taxes, hospitals, and the conduct of officials. Missionaries report on conversions, while civil officers complain about costs and climate. The documents show a colony still taking shape, with Spanish power thin on the ground. Together they give first-hand evidence for Philippine history. The volume suits readers who want sources rather than a single narrative.
13752-wulfric-the-weapon-thane-a-story-o:
Charles W. Whistler set this novel in East Anglia during the Danish conquest of the 800s. Wulfric serves as weapon thane, or armour bearer, to King Eadmund. The story draws on Dunstan's account, passed from a witness, of Eadmund's martyrdom on November 20, 870. Whistler admits records of earlier events are vague and fills gaps with fiction.

Wulfric sails, fights, and watches the Danish host advance after Thetford. Sea spray, shields, and camp talk fill the action scenes. Loyalty to king and faith drives the hero through defeat. The novel blends history with adventure for young readers. It gives a vivid view of Anglo-Saxon England under attack.
14115-quatre-contes-de-prosper-me-rime-e:
F. C. L. Van Steenderen edited four tales by Prosper Mérimée for American students of French, adding an introduction, notes, and a full vocabulary. Mateo Falcone opens in Corsica, where shepherds, maquis scrub, and a code of honor rule the hills. A later tale, Tamango, turns to a slave ship, where captive Africans rise against a captain named Ledoux in a fight across the narrow decks.

Classroom apparatus shapes the volume as much as story. Notes gloss hard words and customs, while the vocabulary at the back defines each term with examples. Students thus read real French prose with a safety net, meeting Corsican vendetta and Atlantic cruelty in the original tongue. Teachers chose Mérimée for clear style and strong plots, and this edition still serves readers moving from exercises to literature.
14235-ma-s-vale-man-a-que-fuerza-proverb:
Manuel Tamayo y Baus wrote Más vale maña que fuerza, a one-act proverb play, here edited for American students by Carlos Everett Conant in 1918. The New-World Spanish Series volume adds notes, composition exercises, and a full vocabulary. Students meet real stage Spanish with a safety net, learning words like cólera, colgar, and comprender in context.

Domestic comedy drives the plot. Elisa forgives Antonio for hiding an innocent caprice, insisting his silence came only from fear of grieving her. She trusts his little heart more than her own, she says, touching his breast. Juanita's bold lying draws Antonio's praise for Elisa's goodness, and the proverb title proves itself: cunning beats force in love and household war. Short, witty, and teachable, the play suits a first Spanish classroom well.
14265-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume nine of the Philippine Islands series, edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, covers 1593 to 1597 from contemporary books and manuscripts. A historical introduction by Edward Gaylord Bourne frames documents on exploration, missions, trade, and government. The second embassy to Japan, letters to Felipe II, and memoranda on troops open the volume.

Governor Gómez Pérez Dasmariñas dominates the record. Fray Francisco de Ortega reports Luzon improving under his vigilance, with peace, good government, and gospel spread advancing rapidly. Royal orders follow on duties: foreigners arriving with food, ammunition, and materials, whether Chinese, Portuguese, Japanese, or Bornean, shall pay no duties on those goods until the king orders otherwise. Proclamations must spread the news widely. Scholars still use the series as a primary source for early colonial Philippines.
14266-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited this tenth volume of The Philippine Islands, covering 1597 to 1599. It prints letters, reports, and records from the early Spanish years in the islands. The editors add notes, and Edward Gaylord Bourne wrote a historical introduction. Governors, friars, and soldiers speak in their own documents. The volume forms part of a vast set that runs from 1493 to 1898.

Letters to King Felipe the Second report on Manila, its hospital, and its trade. One report urges storing rice in the hull, so a town can hold out in a siege without seizing food from natives. Another tells of a punitive raid on Jolo, where Captain Joan Pacho and nineteen soldiers were killed in rain and ambush. The volume shows rule, war, and want in plain official prose. It gives scholars the raw matter of early colonial life.
14510-ireland-under-coercion-the-diary-o:
William Henry Hurlbert's first volume of his Irish diary, in a second edition of 1888, opens with a map and a preface defending his views after barely a month in print. Cardinal Manning's warning about Ireland and the empire fronts the book.

Hurlbert travels through Irish towns and estates, noting evictions, boycotting, and the methods of political combinations he blamed for demoralizing the people. He also recounts older history, from Hugh O'Neill's escape to Kinsale. The diary is a partisan American report, detailed and readable, from the Land War's sharpest years.
14511-ireland-under-coercion-the-diary-o:
William Henry Hurlbert, an American journalist, kept this diary of Ireland under the Coercion Acts, and this second volume, in a second edition of 1888, covers his travels from Rossbehy onward. Hurlbert reported for American readers.

He records evictions at Glenbehy, boycotting, savings-bank deposits, drives through Limerick and Kerry, and talks with priests, landlords, and tenants about rents and arrears. The diary weighs Irish grievances against British law with an outsider's eye. Hurlbert's notes on rents, savings, and trade give the diary lasting value. It remains a detailed, on-the-ground source for the Land War years.
14685-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume eleven of The Philippine Islands, 1493 to 1898, edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, covers 1599 to 1602 with documents, an introduction by Edward Gaylord Bourne, and notes. The series gathered contemporary books and manuscripts.

Documents include Manila Audiencia ordinances, a hospital for Indians, letters from the royal fiscal to the king, and plans for patages loaded with rice, wine, and Sangley earthenware for the Moluccas. The volume shows Spanish colonial rule in trade, law, and missions. It remains a key source for early Philippine history in English. Blair and Robertson edited fifty-five volumes in the series.
15022-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume twelve of The Philippine Islands, 1493 to 1898, covers 1601 to 1604, edited and annotated by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, with a historical introduction by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The series gathers explorations by early navigators, descriptions of islands and peoples, history and records of Catholic missions.

Contemporaneous books and manuscripts show political, economic, commercial and religious conditions from first European contact to the close of the nineteenth century. Documents of 1601 open this volume, with a preface setting them in context. The series remains a standard English source for early Philippine history, translated and annotated for scholars and general readers alike.
15184-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, this thirteenth volume of the Philippine series covers 1604 and 1605. It concludes Chirino's relation of the islands, printed at Rome in 1604. Letters from Manila to Philip III, decrees on religious orders, and a grant to the Jesuit seminary at Cebu follow.

Documents show trade rules with New Spain, mission work, and colonial government in action, with Bourne's notes to guide readers. The volume serves historians of Spain's Pacific empire and of early Philippine life. General readers can dip into letters that feel close to the events they report.
15445-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited this fourteenth volume of The Philippine Islands, covering 1606 to 1609, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The great series prints early navigators' explorations, descriptions of peoples, histories, and Catholic mission records, in contemporary books and manuscripts. It traces political, economic, commercial, and religious life from first European contact to the nineteenth century's close.

Documents here include complaints against the archbishop from Manila in 1605, relations with the Chinese, letters to King Felipe III, and a Dominican mission account. A Dutch factory at Tidore and the Sangley insurrection of 1603 also appear. Read as primary sources, the papers give the colony in its own words: quarrels, trade, missions, and rule, without the smoothing of later history.
15530-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited this seventeenth volume of The Philippine Islands, covering 1609 to 1616, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The series prints contemporary explorations, mission records, and histories, showing political, economic, commercial, and religious life in the islands from first European contact onward.

Documents open with laws on navigation and commerce from 1583 to 1609, Jesuit missions of 1608 and 1609, and a decree regulating services of Filipinos. Later papers include a Recollect petition, a Dominican request to suppress the Audiencia, and letters between Manila, Cavite, and Madrid. The volume gives the colony's early seventeenth century in its own documents, quarrels and all, for readers who want sources rather than summaries.
15564-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited this eighteenth volume of The Philippine Islands, covering 1617 to 1620, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The series prints contemporary explorations, mission records, and histories, showing political, economic, commercial, and religious life from first European contact to the nineteenth century's close.

Documents include a letter to Felipe III from Manila in August 1617. They cover trade between New Spain and the Far East, and events in the Philippines in 1617 and 1618. A description of the islands from Manila in 1618 follows. Dutch factories and posts in the Orient, a memorial on the Manila hospital, and letters between Cavite and Madrid follow. The volume gives the colony's early seventeenth century in its own papers, for readers who want the record, not a retelling.
16086-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne, this 1904 volume is the nineteenth of a fifty-five volume set on the Philippines. It prints, in English, Spanish papers from 1620 and 1621 drawn largely from the archives at Seville. Letters, decrees, and reports from governors, friars, and royal officials make up the contents.

The papers press for reform in the islands: fairer treatment of native people by friars, an end to forced labor, and aid against Dutch ships that threatened Spanish rule. Readers get the colony's troubles in the words of the men who ran it and complained about it. The volume serves students of early colonial rule, missions, and trade in Southeast Asia.
16133-the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-v:
Volume twenty of Blair and Robertson's Philippine Islands series, published in 1904, carries Spanish documents from 1621 to 1624 in English translation. Governors, archbishops, friars, and kings write to one another about a colony under strain. News from the provinces, letters to the king from Fajardo and others, and Franciscan affairs fill the pages. A royal letter to Fajardo in 1623 closes the set. Later papers grant a Dominican college at Manila and send an expedition to the Igorrote mines.

Drawn from archives in Seville and Madrid, the papers show trade, missions, mining, and native resistance through official eyes. Readers gain a close, document-level view of early Spanish rule in Luzon and beyond. The volume suits students of colonial history who want sources, not summaries.
16244-the-turkish-jester-or-the-pleasant:
George Borrow translated these pleasantries of Cogia Nasr Eddin Efendi from the Turkish, printed at Ipswich by W. Webber in 1884. The jests run to a hundred stories of the wise fool who preaches from the pulpit and traps his hearers in their own answers. Asked whether they know what he will say, the crowd says no, and he replies he has nothing to say until they know.

When they claim they do know, he answers that those who know need no sermon, and walks out leaving them to argue which of them knew and which did not. Borrow's plain English keeps the tales short, sly, and easy to retell. Readers who like folk humor will enjoy this classic of Turkish wit.
16501-the-philippine-islands-1493-1803-v:
This fifth volume of the Philippine Islands series, edited by Blair and Robertson, prints documents of 1582 and 1583. Letters to Felipe II from Manila, Loarca's relation of the islands, Salazar's letter, and papal decrees on the Dominicans fill the 1582 papers. Complaints against Penalosa and affairs in the islands follow for 1583.

The series traces the islands from first European contact through contemporary books and manuscripts. This volume gives the early Spanish colony in its own words: governors, friars, and settlers writing home. Historians of the Philippines will find it a primary source of the first rank.
17487-casa-grande-ruin-thirteenth-annual:
Cosmos Mindeleff wrote this report on Casa Grande ruin for the thirteenth annual report of the Bureau of Ethnology. Its contents run from introduction, location, character, history, and literature, through description of the Casa Grande group and the ruin itself, to state of preservation, dimensions, and detailed description. Openings and conclusions close the paper, with plates including a map of the group.

Readers get a precise, measured account of one of the Southwest's great prehistoric structures, before its later repair. Mindeleff's report shows early American archaeology at work, recording walls, rooms, and decay. It remains a key source for Casa Grande and for Hohokam architecture.
17923-the-visions-of-england-lyrics-on-l:
Francis T. Palgrave wrote The Visions of England in 1889, printed by Cassell in London, Paris, New York, and Melbourne. Palgrave, professor of poetry at Oxford, here gives seventy lyrics on leading men and events in English history.

The poems move through kings, saints, soldiers, and turns of fate, from early days to modern times, each lyric a small, vivid scene. Palgrave also edited the famed Golden Treasury, and his taste for clear, musical verse shows here. It is a stately, patriotic song-book of England, best read as Victorian verse history, not as strict fact.
18049-the-diary-of-an-ennuye-e:
Mrs. Jameson wrote The Diary of an Ennuyée, printed in Paris in 1836 by Baudry's European Library. Jameson, author of Visits and Sketches at Home and Abroad, here gives a young lady's diary of her first tour on the Continent.

The diary opens at Calais on June 21, where the traveler calls for French pens and ink, and opens her morocco-bound diary with its Bramah lock. Classical memories, threadbare raptures, and poetical effusions follow, in the voice of a bored, bright girl. It is a witty, melancholy travel book, and a fine portrait of a young woman's Grand Tour.
18189-growing-nuts-in-the-north-a-person:
Carl Weschcke wrote this personal account of thirty-three years growing nuts in Minnesota and Wisconsin. Weschcke published it at St. Paul in 1953, with copyright in 1954, and he stresses both his failures and his final successes. Few books, he says, treated nut trees for cold climates, so he set down what he had learned for the amateur grower.

Chapters take up first encounters, black walnuts, hazels and filberts, pecans and hybrids, hickory, butternut, and English walnuts in Wisconsin. Later chapters cover pests, seed storage, planting, winter protection of grafts, grafting methods, and hybridizing. Readers get practical northern advice from long trial: which trees bear, which fail, and how to coax a crop where winters are hard.
19817-the-heroic-enthusiasts-gli-eroici-:
Giordano Bruno published Gli Eroici Furori, The Heroic Enthusiasts, in London in 1585. Part the first appears here in English dress. Its apparatus praises Nola, Bruno's home town in Italy. Nola was conspicuous for culture from Roman times onward. Its people were noted for courtesy, valor, and keen perception. They loved philosophy, the introduction insists.

Bruno's dialogues praise heroic love that strains toward the divine. They mix sonnets, argument, and cosmic daring. Bruno was later burned for heresy in Rome in 1600. His infinite-worlds vision ran through works like this. The English edition served Victorian readers curious about him. Part one opens a difficult, blazing book.
24613-the-negro-and-the-nation-a-history:
George S. Merriam wrote this history of American slavery and enfranchisement, first published in 1906 and reprinted at New York in 1970. Its chapters trace how slavery grew in America, the acts of the fathers, conflict and compromise, and the widening rift between North and South.

Later chapters treat Calhoun and Garrison, Birney, Channing, and Webster, and the underlying forces that drove the nation to war and then to emancipation. Merriam writes as a historian of the generation after the Civil War. His book remains a solid, readable survey of slavery's growth, the struggle against it, and freedom's first years.
2630-the-interpreters-of-genesis-and-the:
Thomas Henry Huxley steps between two fighters in this fourth essay from Science and Hebrew Tradition. A fabulist warns those who interpose in quarrels, he notes, and he knows the risk of standing between so powerful a controversialist as Gladstone and the divine Gladstone attacks.

Huxley judges both sides, asking what Genesis interpreters claim and what interpreters of nature actually show. His tone is cool, legal, and amused, and his verdict favors evidence over authority. The essay stands as a classic of Victorian debate, and a defense of science's right to speak.
26318-the-horsewoman-a-practical-guide-t:
Alice M. Hayes's Horsewoman, here in a second edition revised and enlarged in 1903, is a practical guide to side-saddle riding. Hayes, author of My Leper Friends, drew on seven years riding hundreds of horses in India, Ceylon, Egypt, China, and South Africa. She served as rough-rider at her husband's horse-breaking classes, and M. Horace Hayes edited the volume.

Later experience hunting in Leicestershire and Cheshire, plus teaching many pupils, shaped the new edition with 133 photographic pictures. Chapters teach seat, saddle grip, trot, and canter, with care for a nervous horse. A pupil who fears the trot returns to the walk, then tries short trots with praise. The book speaks from hard, hands-on practice.
3399-complete-project-gutenberg-william-:
This Project Gutenberg file collects William Dean Howells's essays on literature into one volume. It brings together his studies of books and authors, including My Literary Passions and Criticism and Fiction, with related pieces on reading and taste. The file is a compilation made for electronic reading, not a book Howells published in this exact form during his life.

Inside, Howells writes about the writers who shaped him, from Cervantes and Goldsmith to Dickens and Thackeray, and about what makes a novel honest. He argues for fiction that stays close to common life rather than chasing grand effects. The collection serves as a guide to his critical mind and as a shelf of short essays for readers who love books about books.
4975-spinifex-and-sand-a-narrative-of-fi:
David Carnegie's Spinifex and Sand narrates five years of pioneering and exploration in Western Australia, from early days in the colony to prospecting rushes and desert travel. Chapters follow a miner on Bayley's first expedition, the rush to Kurnalpi, and the push to Queen Victoria Spring and unknown country.

Portable condensers, granite rocks, namma holes, and soaks mark the desert's water lore, while camel fights, gold at Lake Darlot, and lonely bush travel test the party. Carnegie writes as a prospector who lived the hardship he describes. Readers get a firsthand account of the goldfields frontier, hard, dry, and vividly told.
5709-la-vende-e:
Anthony Trollope's La Vendee is a historical romance of the royalist rising in western France during the Revolution. It opens by refusing a fresh description of Paris in the summer of 1792. The sacking of the palace on the tenth of August is already well known. So is the king's refuge in the National Assembly. The story then turns to the Poitevins, the peasants and nobles who rose in the Vendee.

The tale follows a region at war with Paris, where loyalty, faith, and local pride clash with revolutionary power. Trollope writes with his usual steady attention to character, letting political choice play out in households and villages. The novel suits readers of historical fiction who want the Revolution seen from its provinces, through people caught between king, republic, and home.
63-the-number-e:
Mathematicians sometimes need the constant e to far more digits than a pocket calculator gives. This file lists e to about 100,000 decimal places, computed on a Cray Y-MP supercomputer. The method used Brent's multiple-precision routines from 1978.

First the alternating series for 1 over e was summed, taking about 594 seconds. Inverting that result took about 97 more seconds. No special tuning beyond the compiler's default vectorization was tried. The file serves as a raw reference for computation and checking. Programmers and students still use such long digit strings to test arithmetic and software.
8145-life-and-times-of-washington-volume:
John F. Schroeder began this life and times of Washington, and after his death Benson John Lossing completed it; the 1903 source title page names only Schroeder-Lossing. This revised, enlarged, and enriched second volume, with an introduction by Edward C. Towne, covers part four: Washington as Continental commander-in-chief, 1775 to 1783. Its chapters include Lord Howe outgeneralled, Washington holding Howe in check, Burgoyne's defeat and surrender, Valley Forge, and the battle of Monmouth.

The volume combines biography with military history, following Washington through the Revolution's middle years. Lossing's illustrations and detail give the narrative a documentary richness. For readers of Washington biography, it remains a substantial nineteenth-century account, valuable both for its facts and for its period view of the founding general.
9175-the-art-of-poetry-an-epistle-to-the:
George Colman translated Horace's Art of Poetry, the Epistle to the Pisos, with notes, printed in London in 1783. Horace, the Roman poet, advises young writers on unity, decorum, and the craft of verse. Colman dedicates his version to two Warton schoolmasters, Joseph and Thomas, friends from talk about Horace.

The epistle warns against purple patches, mixed genres, and faults of taste, in lines poets still quote. Colman's notes gloss the Latin for English readers, with care for sense and style. The book remains a classic guide to writing well, from antiquity to the Augustan age.
complete-project-gutenberg-william-dean-:
William Dean Howells's literary essays and memoirs are gathered in this compilation, issued by Project Gutenberg under the title Of Literature, Entire. Howells wrote all three books bundled here. Together they cover his friendships, his reading, and his critical creed. The set forms a compact library of his nonfiction.

Literary Friends and Acquaintance recalls the poets and scholars Howells knew in Cambridge and Boston. Literature and Life collects shorter studies of American scenes and literary business. My Literary Passions tells what books formed him as a boy. Criticism and Fiction, joined with it, argues for honest realism in novels. Readers meet Howells the critic and memoirist whole, explaining both the writers he loved and the standards he urged on American fiction.
doe-osti-17010948-direct-carbon-conversi: Baking captured carbon into concrete got its DOE write-up, and this report covers conversion to cementitious materials. The research turns a pollutant into pavement. Builders get a greener recipe. The conversion was studied. The recipe was greener. The study was DOE's.

The pages assess whether the physics works. The experimenters get their green light or red. The study was feasibility. The light was green or red.
doe-osti-2571203-providence-performing-a: A Providence theater got an energy makeover, and this DOE report tracks the efficiency retrofits. The pages detail the upgrades and savings. The managers get their playbook. The playbook was PPAC. The savings were detailed. The theater was Providence's. The makeover was energy.
doe-osti-2575016-self-healable-copolymer: Self-healing hydrogen hoses got their DOE composites, and this report covers copolymer hoses for H2 dispensing. The pages detail the healable design. The fueling stations get their hose. The hoses were self-healable. The stations were fueling. The design was healable.
doe-osti-2585476-addendum-to-sand2023-09: Xyce's transmission line model got its addendum, and this DOE text verifies the lumped-element model. The pages detail the Empire-Cable support. The circuit modelers get their update. The model was lumped-element. The verification was transmission line. The support was Empire-Cable.
doe-osti-2586384-assessing-the-impact-of: Wind turbine lubrication got its impact assessment, and this CRADA report covers efficiency and economics. The pages detail the fleet study. The wind operators get their numbers. The fleet was US wind. The study was fleet. The operators got numbers.
doe-osti-2587455-optimization-of-scrap-m: Scrap melting with electric arcs got optimized, and this DOE report covers steel manufacturing. The pages detail the arc optimization. The steelmakers get their method. The arc was electric. The manufacturing was steel. The makers got methods. The steel was manufactured.
doe-osti-2588549-considerations-for-a-me: Medium-voltage DC electrolysis got its testbed considerations, and this DOE text lays out the design factors. The pages detail the planning. The hydrogen engineers get their guide. The testbed was medium-voltage DC. The guide was testbed. The factors were design.
doe-osti-2589119-cyclic-olefin-copolymer: Tough plastic membranes for fuel cells got their DOE recipe, and this report covers the reinforced polymers. The pages detail the chemistry. The fuel cell folks get their data. The plastic was cyclic olefin. The chemistry was detailed. The data were fuel cell.

doe-osti-3374965-connected-residential-c: Imagine a neighborhood where homes, solar panels, and batteries act as one team with the power company. This final report covers connected residential communities designed for resilience — keeping power flowing in outages — with benefits for both customers and utilities. doe-osti-3377852-adaptive-cybersecurity-: Rooftop solar and batteries are great until hackers turn them against the grid. The AdCyDER project builds adaptive cybersecurity for these distributed energy resources, using reinforcement learning to tune defenses on the fly. The defenses even anticipate the attacker's next move — a chess game played by machines.
doe-osti-3403346-halau-uma-kahikinui-com: On Maui's remote southeastern slopes, the Kahikinui community is planning a cultural, learning, and resilience center called Halau Uma. govdocs-archive_org-nsia-BrenerMiltonE_B: nsia-BrenerMiltonE Brener Milton E: the made public government document on Milton Brener, captured as titled. Subject: government records. A bare file, kept as issued. An obscure item, of the files. From the archive shelves, for readers.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-KuenzliAlfredE_: A letter dated December 17, 1969, thanks Alfred E. Kuenzli for sending a clipping from the St. Louis Post-Dispatch. The clipping concerned Nazi party activities. The writer's signature cannot be recovered from the text, so the letter survives without its author. What remains shows two private citizens exchanging newspaper material about the American far right at the end of the 1960s, and one of them keeping the clipping on file.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-McDervidHaroldE:
Special Agent Richard E. Harrison of the FBI's Dallas office wrote this memorandum about a telegram. The telegram had been sent to Lee Harvey Oswald by Harold E. McDervid, a Chicago attorney. It was never delivered. Harrison's memo records that fact for the Oswald file.

An undelivered telegram is a small thing, but the bureau logged it like everything else touching Oswald. Who was writing to him, from where, and why, were questions agents pursued for months. The memo does not give the telegram's text. It preserves the sender's name and city, the failure of delivery, and the bureau's decision that the item belonged in the record.
hume-history-of-england-1860-part-e:
David Hume's History of England moves through Part E, the fifth of six parts in the 1860 Virtue edition. The history itself belongs to 1754 through 1762, when Hume issued its volumes one by one. He had planned it as a cure for party rage: a past told whole, with blame and praise shared out fairly.

As the parts advance, England's story grows tenser, through civil war and the fall of a king. Hume's prose never hurries, and his judgments, cool and dry, still start arguments. The complete work counts seventy-one chapters, from Caesar's landing to the settlement of 1688. Part E brings that long arc near its close.
la-vende-e:
Anthony Trollope's La Vendée is a historical romance of the French Revolution. Its contents run across three volumes. Early chapters name St. Florent, Durbellière, Cathelineau, and de Lescure.

The story follows royalist fighters in the Vendée region of France. Councils of war, recruiting, and battles fill the middle chapters. Later ones reach Saumur, a sentence of death, and even Robespierre. Trollope builds fiction from real leaders and places. Readers get a vivid, partisan view of a civil war that split families and villages. Trollope wrote it early, before his Barsetshire fame. The Vendée war gave his young pen battles, faith, and loyalty to test.
life-and-times-of-washington-volume-2-re:
Volume Two of this Washington life came from Schroeder and Lossing. John Frederick Schroeder began it; Benson John Lossing completed it. Edward C. Towne added a special introduction to this revised edition. Part Four covers Washington as Continental commander-in-chief, 1775 to 1783.

Chapters follow Valley Forge, Monmouth, and Arnold's treason. Washington outgenerals Howe and holds him in check. Burgoyne's defeat and surrender mark a turning point. Southern campaigns close the volume's story of the Revolutionary War. Washington directs a descent on Rhode Island in one chapter. Operations in northern and southern states alternate through the volume.
ma-s-vale-man-a-que-fuerza-proverbio-en-:
Más vale maña que fuerza is a Spanish one-act play by Manuel Tamayo y Baus. Its title is a proverb: skill is worth more than strength. This school edition came from the World Book Company in 1918. Carlos Everett Conant added notes, exercises, and a vocabulary.

The book belongs to the New-World Spanish Series for American students. Tamayo y Baus was one of Spain's leading dramatists. His short comedy turns on wit defeating brute force. Students read the play, then drill composition from its scenes. The edition shows how Spanish was taught a century ago. It remains a pleasant first step into Spanish theater.
nasa-tm-19650025609-self-induced-balloon:
Harold N Murrow and Robert M Henry at Langley studied a problem that sounds odd at first. A balloon used to measure wind can itself sway and bob. Those self-induced motions then distort the very wind data it collects. The pair presented their work at a meteorology meeting in Atlantic City.

A drifting balloon is assumed to move with the wind. Any extra motion of its own adds false signal. Murrow and Henry examine where that extra motion comes from and how it affects readings. Their findings help weather services judge how much to trust balloon wind data, a daily input to forecasts.
nasa-tm-19670006714-tables-of-thermionic:
Kenneth Carr, of Rose Polytechnic Institute in Terre Haute, Indiana, compiled these tables during a 1966 summer fellowship at NASA's Lewis Research Center. Thermionic emission is the release of electrons from a hot material. The tables gather the thermionic and related electric properties of the elements and compounds.

Carr says he compiled the values for people working in emission physics. He warns readers that the listed values were checked only quickly. Anyone using a value should confirm it in the original reference first. That honest caution makes the tables a starting point for research, not a final authority.
nasa-tm-19690008779-computer-analysis-of:
C. H. Ehrmann and D. V. Reames of Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this November 1968 preprint on computer analysis of particle tracks in nuclear emulsion. Nuclear emulsion is a photographic material that records the paths of fast charged particles as lines of tiny grains. Reading those tracks by eye under a microscope is slow, painstaking work.

Their system points a television camera through the microscope and digitizes its signal to detect developed grains. The data flow in real time to a computer, which picks out grains lying in a track. It then sums grain volumes and computes measures of their spread. A rotating prism lets the system analyze tracks running at any angle through the emulsion.
nasa-tm-19690029175-dynamical-performanc:
David L. Blanchard of Goddard Space Flight Center reports the dynamical performance of RAE-A, also called Explorer 38, in this May 1969 paper, X-723-69-214. RAE-A was a radio astronomy satellite that unfolded very long antennas in orbit. It then settled into place by gravity-gradient capture, using Earth's pull to hold its attitude.

Blanchard compares an in-orbit simulator against the real spacecraft's behavior, stage by stage. Figures trace roll, pitch, and yaw as the antennas deploy first to four hundred fifty feet. Later stages reach six hundred and then seven hundred fifty feet. Each stage pairs simulated motion beside observed motion. Time spent in Earth's shadow per orbit is also tracked throughout.
nasa-tm-19710006972-very-long-baseline-i:
J. Ramasastry and two co-workers at the Goddard Space Flight Center wrote this preprint on very long baseline interferometry. The method links distant antennas so they act as one huge instrument. Their experiments used the ATS-3 and ATS-5 satellites as signal sources, rather than distant stars.

Strictly, the document is a proposal, made jointly with the Smithsonian Astrophysical Observatory. Measurements would run at two radio bands, one satellite serving each band. The aim is to judge the method as a high precision tracking technique for spacecraft. The same readings could serve geodesy, fixing station locations, polar motion, and continental drift, and would help compute the satellites' own orbits.
podcast-dannyjones-AaDq8g7II_E:
Author Annie Jacobsen writes narrative histories of America's secret programs, built from interviews and declassified files. With Danny Jones, she discusses the reporting behind her work on the Pentagon's nuclear war plans: the documents and testimony describing how a nuclear war would actually be ordered, launched, and fought.

Jacobsen's method is to reconstruct minutes. Her nuclear work follows a single scenario through the real chain of command, using the government's own planning record. Jones draws out the most sobering findings, including how little time leaders would have to decide. Unlike most guests in this series, Jacobsen brings a paper trail that can be checked, and the episode's dread comes from documents rather than claims. It is one of the most grounded hours in the collection.
quatre-contes-de-prosper-me-rime-e:
Quatre Contes brings together four tales by Prosper Mérimée in French, edited with an introduction, notes, and vocabulary by F. C. L. van Steenderen of Lake Forest University and published in New York by Henry Holt and Company. The notes and word list mark it as a school edition for students reading French.

The first tale, Mateo Falcone, opens on the road out of Porto-Vecchio in Corsica, climbing toward the maquis, the thick brush that shelters shepherds and any man at odds with the law. Footnotes explain hard words and places as the prose moves into the hills.
spinifex-and-sand-a-narrative-of-five-ye:
David W. Carnegie tells his five years in Spinifex and Sand. He spent them on the goldfields of Western Australia. He spent them in its far inner parts as well. Carnegie lived from 1871 to 1900. He gives the book to his mother. A line on honest tales plainly told heads it. His first note calls the pages a faithful tale. Readers who want wild escapes should look away, he warns.

The Australian bush sets man against nature alone. Death from thirst hangs over the traveler always. Hostile blacks attack at rare times. No rare game cheers the way. No broad lakes or winding rivers please the eye. One sameness of dry country must be faced. Nature asks toil at each step. Carnegie hopes readers will glean the pioneers' hardships. He hopes they will see more in a gold seeker. The mere lust of gold is not the whole spur, he holds.
the-art-of-poetry-an-epistle-to-the-piso:
George Colman turned Horace's Epistle to the Pisos, the famous Art of Poetry, into English with notes, printed at London for T. Cadell in the Strand in 1783. A letter at the front addresses the Reverend Joseph Warton, master of Winchester School, and the Reverend Thomas Warton of Trinity College, Oxford, as dear friends.

Colman tells them a talk some months before revived a long-held plan: to share his thoughts on Horace's epistle with the public. He had dropped the plan for want of time and will to make a version he thought must go with the Latin. The letter itself, warm and slightly sly about whether his friends agreed with him, serves as his preface.
the-diary-of-an-ennuye-e:
Mrs. Jameson, author of Visits and Sketches at Home and Abroad, wrote The Diary of an Ennuyee, shown here in a new edition printed at Paris by Baudry's European Library in 1836. A motto from Spenser heads the title page, describing a maid sad, solemn, and full of frail fancies, who knew not what ailed her and thought it not love but some melancholy.

The diary opens at Calais on June 21. The writer asks what young lady, on her first trip to the Continent, would not keep a diary. No sooner have we slept on the shores of France, she begins, no sooner are we seated in the gay salon, than the record starts.
the-interpreters-of-genesis-and-the-inte:
Thomas Henry Huxley steps into a quarrel in this essay. It is essay four from Science and Hebrew Tradition. Mr. Gladstone and the scholar M. Reville are the combatants. Their subject is the worth of Genesis as science. Huxley opens with the fabulist's warning. Those who interpose in quarrels risk a beating. He admits Reville can defend himself well. Two excuses still move him to write.

A foreigner stands little chance with English readers, he argues. Gladstone's authority and rhetoric are too strong. Huxley casts himself as an uncommissioned science proctor. The Queen's proctor serves justice in the same way. Science questions are at stake here too. Neither fighter speaks as an expert in them. Huxley offers forty years of study as his warrant. He praises Reville's book for its fair, respectful judgment.
the-number-e:
A long list of digits gives the value of the mathematical constant e to about 100,000 places. The figures were computed on an NCSA Cray Y-MP computer using Brent's multiple precision routines, a method printed in 1978. The work first computed the alternating series for 1/e, then inverted that result to get e itself.

The computing took about 594 seconds for the series and about 97 seconds for the inversion, with no special tuning beyond the compiler's default work. Page after page of digits follows, starting 2.7182818284. The list serves readers who need e stated far beyond the few places used in daily work.
the-philippine-islands-1493-1803-volume-: Volume I of The Philippine Islands covers 1493 to 1529. It opens a series of fifty-five volumes of old records. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added the historical introduction and notes. The series title in the pages present reads 1493-1898, though the record's heading gives 1493-1803. Front matter and contents alone are present here, so the documents themselves do not appear. The contents list the papal bulls of 1493, the Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494, and the Junta of Badajoz of 1524.

Volume II of The Philippine Islands covers 1521 to 1569. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series of old records. Edward Gaylord Bourne added the introduction and notes. The pages present hold the series title page and contents only, so the documents themselves do not appear. The contents sum up four voyages. Garcia de Loaisa, Alvaro de Saavedra, and Ruy Lopez de Villalobos sailed first. Miguel Lopez de Legazpi came last. His act of taking possession at Cibabao in 1565 and his letters to Felipe II are also listed.

Volume III of The Philippine Islands covers 1569 to 1576. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. Here the reader gets the series title page and contents, not the documents themselves. The list groups letters and reports by year. Legazpi's account of the islands and his letters to Felipe II belong to 1569. The voyage to Luzon belongs to 1570, with the taking of Luzon at Manila. Papers of 1571-72 close the list.

Volume IV of The Philippine Islands covers 1576 to 1582. Blair and Robertson edited the series. This opening holds the series title page, a contents list, and a list of pictures. The records themselves do not appear. The contents name trips to Borneo, Jolo, and Mindanao under Francisco de Sande in 1578-79. Church posts at Manila filled in 1580 come next. Letters to Felipe II from Ronquillo de Penalosa follow, dated 1581 and 1582. A rule limiting departures from the islands is also listed.

Volume V of The Philippine Islands covers 1582 to 1583. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. Title page and contents are what the opening offers; the documents themselves do not appear. Listed papers include Loarca's account of the islands from 1582. Letters from Governor Penalosa and Fray Domingo de Salazar appear too. Papal decrees on the Dominicans are named. The 1583 founding of the Audiencia of Manila closes the list shown.
the-philippine-islands-1493-1898-volume-:
Volume VI of The Philippine Islands, covering 1583 to 1588, carries an editorial announcement that changed the whole series. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson explain that the work was first planned to end at the beginning of the nineteenth century. Subscribers and reviewers pressed for more, so the series now runs to 1898, the close of Spanish rule, under the new title The Philippine Islands: 1493-1898.

The editors promise to hold the series to fifty-five volumes, using space saved in the original plan. The early history stays full, while the nineteenth century will be shown through decrees, reports, and official documents. Space limits, closed archives, and the classic period argument had shaped the old plan, and the announcement answers each in turn.

Volume VII of The Philippine Islands, 1588 to 1591, continues the series edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The opening gives the series title page and contents; the documents themselves lie beyond it. Papers of 1588 include relations and letters from Domingo de Salazar and Santiago de Vera. For 1589 the list names a conspiracy against the Spaniards, royal instructions to Gomez Perez Dasmarinas, and Juan de Plasencia's Customs of the Tagalogs.

Volume VIII of The Philippine Islands covers 1591 to 1593. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. What is present is the series title page with its contents list; the documents themselves do not appear. The list names the gathering of tributes in the islands. A papal grant of freedom to the Indians dates to 1591. A contract for the conquest of Mindanao, an account of the encomiendas, and papers on the defense of Manila are also listed.

Volume IX of The Philippine Islands covers 1593 to 1597. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. Series title page and contents are present; the documents themselves are not. The contents list the second embassy to Japan in 1593. Letters from both Dasmarinas governors to Felipe II appear. A letter to the king of Camboja and a check on the Manila hospital are named. A reply to the Japanese emperor's letter, from 1594, closes the list shown.

Volume X of The Philippine Islands covers 1597 to 1599. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. The opening holds the series title page and contents alone; the documents themselves do not appear. Listed papers include Antonio de Morga's letters and his 1598 report on conditions. Francisco Tello's letters to Felipe II appear too. The welcome of the royal seal at Manila is named. Letters from the archbishop of Manila and the bishop of Nueva Segovia close the list.

Volume XI of The Philippine Islands covers 1599 to 1602. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. Series title page and contents make up what is present; the documents themselves do not appear. The list names rules made by the Audiencia of Manila. A hospital for Indians at Manila and a letter from the king of Borneo to Governor Tello appear. The calming of Mindanao and Oliver van Noordt's attack on Luzon in 1600 are listed, with Morga's report on the Dutch fight.

Volume XII of The Philippine Islands covers 1601 to 1604. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. The pages present give title page and contents, not the documents themselves. Contents cover a trip to the Malucas and papers on Philippine trade. Three Chinese mandarins at Manila in 1603 are named. The Sangley rising is listed too. Pedro Chirino's account of the islands, from 1604, begins here.

Volume XIII of The Philippine Islands covers 1604 to 1605. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. Title page and contents are present here; the documents themselves do not appear. The volume ends Chirino's account of 1604. Letters from Governor Acuna come next. Decrees on religious orders and on trade with Nueva Espana are listed. Complaints against the Chinese in 1605 and a letter from a Chinese official to Acuna close the list.

Volume XIV of The Philippine Islands covers 1606 to 1609. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. What the opening offers is the series title page and contents; the documents themselves do not appear. Listed items include complaints against the archbishop in 1605. The Dominican mission of 1606 and the Dutch factory at Tidore appear. The Sangley rising of 1603, retold in 1606, is named. Papers on Chinese settlement in the islands close the list shown.

Volume XVII of The Philippine Islands covers 1609 to 1616. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. Series title page and contents are what is present; the documents themselves do not appear. The list includes laws on sailing and trade. Jesuit missions of 1608-09 are named. A decree on services owed by Filipinos appears. The 1611 founding of the college of Santo Tomas at Manila is listed, with letters between Felipe III and Governor Juan de Silva.

Volume XVIII of The Philippine Islands covers 1617 to 1620. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. The opening holds title page and contents only; the documents themselves do not appear. Listed papers include events in the islands in 1617-18. A word picture of the islands from 1618 appears. Dutch posts in the East and a warning that the Dutch threatened the islands are named. A 1619 paper on Philippine ships and shipbuilding closes the list shown.

Volume XIX of The Philippine Islands covers 1620 to 1621. Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson edited the series. Edward Gaylord Bourne added notes. What is present is the title page, a list of pictures, and the start of the contents. The documents themselves do not appear. Items named include reforms needed in the islands, by Hernando de los Rios Coronel. A decree ordering better treatment of the Indians by the friars appears. Forced service by the Indians and letters of Governor Fajardo are also named.

Volume XX of The Philippine Islands, 1621 to 1624, continues the series edited by Emma Helen Blair and James Alexander Robertson, with notes by Edward Gaylord Bourne. The pages present are front matter and a partial contents list; the documents themselves do not appear. Items named include a 1623 letter from Felipe IV to Fajardo, royal permission for the Dominican college in Manila, and a 1624 expedition to the mines of the Igorrotes. Illustrations show Igorrote weapons and the signatures of officials.
the-turkish-jester-or-the-pleasantries-o:
George Borrow translated The Turkish Jester, the pleasantries of Cogia Nasr Eddin Efendi, printed at Ipswich in 1884 and reissued in the 1924 Norwich edition. The first story shows the Cogia mounting the pulpit and asking whether the congregation knows what he will say. When they say no, he asks what he should say to people who do not know. When next they say yes, he answers that some already know, so why speak. A third time he proposes that those who know teach those who do not.

More jests follow: gratitude that God gave the camel no wings, lest camels perch on houses and tumble chimneys onto heads, and the Cogia's astronomy of two identical skies. Borrow, the great linguist of Lavengro, carried these Nasreddin tales into English with dry relish. They remain the Middle East's favourite fool-sage at his most unanswerable.
the-visions-of-england-lyrics-on-leading: Francis T. Palgrave, professor of poetry at Oxford, published The Visions of England with Cassell and Company in 1889. The subtitle describes seventy lyrics on leading men and events in English history. The pages present here give the title page and a long list of Palgrave's other books, so the lyrics themselves do not appear. That list names his Lyrical Poems and Original Hymns, plus editions he prepared of the Golden Treasury, Herrick, Keats, and Tennyson. Readers learn the volume's scope from this record alone.
the-young-engineers-in-colorado-or-at-ra:
H. Irving Hancock's The Young Engineers in Colorado follows Tom Reade and Harry Hazelton to a railroad camp. Its contents promise Bad Pete, doctored field notes, and plots by a man named Black. Chapter one finds Harry thrilled by a real westerner. Tom turns from studying a distant sharp view. The cub engineers have just reached camp. Real work, and real testing by older hands, awaits them.

Twenty-four chapters carry the boys toward a charter-saving finish. Sabotage and a sheriff's intervention raise the stakes. Hancock wrote many such series books for boys. Railroad building supplies danger and technical flavor. Resourceful teenagers outwit grown villains throughout the Gridley boys' adventures.
wulfric-the-weapon-thane-a-story-of-the-:
Charles W. Whistler wrote this story of the Danish conquest of East Anglia. His preface explains the tale of King Eadmund's armour bearer, or weapon thane. Saint Dunstan had the story from the witness himself. Eadmund was killed on November 20, 870, after defeat at Thetford. Local legends of a king's oak and a gold bridge fill gaps in the record.

Whistler also uses Roger of Wendover's version of the traitor Beorn. That treachery, in the tale, brought Ingvar and Hubba down on East Anglia. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle supplies the broad outline. Readers get martyrdom, loyalty, and invasion woven into historical fiction.
